skills.presentation: Foreign body sensation, burning, itching, photophobia, and tearing in the eyes, with eyelid swelling; conjunctival hyperemia (prominent in the fornix and palpebral conjunctiva, bright red, worsening closer to the fornix); increased abnormal discharge (bacterial: copious purulent or mucopurulent discharge that mats the eyelids shut in the morning; viral: watery serous discharge; allergic: thick, stringy discharge accompanied by intense ocular itching).

first_questions: How many days have you had eye redness (red eye), gritty pain, and tearing? Is it in one eye or both eyes?

Is there a lot of eye discharge (eye mucus)? What does it look like? (Is it yellow purulent discharge that mats the eyes shut and makes them hard to open, watery clear tears, or stringy white discharge?)
Are your eyes severely itchy? (to distinguish allergic conjunctivitis)
followup_questions: Has your vision decreased significantly or become blurred? (to differentiate keratitis, glaucoma, and uveitis)
Has any family member, classmate, or coworker around you had the same red eye? Did you go to a swimming pool before symptoms started?
Did you wear contact lenses or corneal contact lenses before symptoms started?
stop_conditions: Clinical subtype of conjunctivitis has been determined (acute bacterial, epidemic viral, or allergic).
It has been confirmed that vision is not impaired, and keratitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and uveitis have been excluded.
History of exposure to infectious sources and contact lens wear is clear.

essential: Ophthalmologic slit-lamp microscopy examination (to observe palpebral conjunctival follicles, papillae, distribution of conjunctival hyperemia, corneal clarity, and anterior chamber status)
Visual acuity testing (uncorrected and corrected visual acuity—to screen for blinding eye diseases)
if_suspected: Gram stain of conjunctival sac discharge smear and bacterial culture plus antimicrobial susceptibility testing (for refractory or severe fulminant purulent conjunctivitis)
Corneal fluorescein staining (to assess for concurrent punctate corneal epithelial loss or corneal ulcer)
avoid: Directly ordering head CT or high-field orbital MRI without performing slit-lamp examination
Prescribing systemic intravenous antibiotic infusion for simple mild viral conjunctivitis

first_line: Symptomatic medication according to etiology: for acute bacterial conjunctivitis, use broad-spectrum antibiotic eye drops (levofloxacin eye drops, tobramycin eye drops) applied frequently, and apply antibiotic eye ointment (erythromycin/tobramycin eye ointment) at bedtime
For viral conjunctivitis, use ganciclovir eye drops/ophthalmic gel
For allergic conjunctivitis, use antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers (olopatadine hydrochloride eye drops, azelastine eye drops)
For patients with copious discharge, the conjunctival sac may be irrigated with normal saline
Do not patch the affected eye under any circumstances.
safety_warnings: Patching or covering the affected eye is strictly prohibited in acute conjunctivitis (patching raises conjunctival sac temperature and allows discharge to accumulate, worsening bacterial proliferation and spread to the cornea)

Glucocorticoid eye drops are contraindicated in herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis/keratitis; before a definitive diagnosis is made, do not casually misuse steroid eye drops (to prevent induced glaucoma and corneal ulcer perforation)
Acute infectious red eye is highly contagious by contact; the patient's towels and washbasins must be strictly isolated and disinfected, and hand hygiene must be strict
personalization: Fulminant hyperacute bacterial conjunctivitis (gonococcal): requires systemic high-dose ceftriaxone sodium injection combined with copious local normal saline irrigation

Severe allergic conjunctivitis with corneal infiltrates: a short course of low-concentration, low-potency steroid eye drops (e.g., fluorometholone eye drops) may be used under ophthalmologist guidance
Long-term contact lens wearers: must immediately stop wearing contact lenses until inflammation is completely cured

skills.presentation: Painless, progressive vision decline, blurred vision, dim or yellowish vision, monocular diplopia or polyopia, glare and photophobia, reduced contrast sensitivity, and sudden increase in pre-existing myopia (in older adults, a false impression that pre-existing presbyopia has 'improved' and they can see small print clearly); examination shows varying degrees of lens opacity and decreased or absent fundal red reflex.

first_questions: How long have you had blurred vision and decreased eyesight? Is it in one eye or both eyes?
Has your vision declined gradually over several years, or did you suddenly lose vision within a few days?
Do you usually have redness or swelling of the eyes, eye pain or pressure, or nausea and headache?
followup_questions: When looking at bright places or at car headlights at night, do you have noticeable glare, dazzling light, or double vision when looking at a single object?
Do you have a history of diabetes, high myopia, ocular trauma, or long-term oral/topical steroid medication use?
How much does your current blurred vision affect your daily life, such as grocery shopping, cooking, reading, and watching TV?
stop_conditions: The course of painless progressive vision loss and the degree of visual function impairment have been clarified
Glaucoma, retinal detachment, macular degeneration, and other acute blinding eye diseases have been ruled out
Systemic history of diabetes and surgical indication assessment are clear

essential: Visual acuity testing (uncorrected visual acuity and best-corrected visual acuity, BCVA)
Slit-lamp microscopy examination (after pupil dilation, identify the location of lens opacity: cortical, nuclear, posterior subcapsular, and opacity grading by LOCS III)
Intraocular pressure measurement (NCT non-contact tonometer, to screen for secondary glaucoma)
Dilated fundus examination (to assess the health of the retina and macular region)
if_suspected: Ophthalmic A/B-scan ultrasonography (to assess axial length and posterior segment vitreoretinal status, especially when severe lens opacity prevents fundus visualization)
Ophthalmic IOL-Master optical biometry (accurate measurement of corneal curvature, anterior chamber depth, and axial length for calculating intraocular lens power)
Corneal endothelial cell microscopy and counting (to assess corneal endothelial functional capacity to tolerate surgery)
avoid: Blindly ordering high-dose systemic CT or MRI scans for a diagnosis of simple cataract
Blindly performing premature forced surgery for mild cataract that does not affect daily life

first_line: Surgery is the only definitive and effective curative treatment: first choice is phacoemulsification cataract extraction combined with foldable intraocular lens (IOL) implantation (minimally invasive incision, rapid recovery)
For early mild cataract, follow-up observation may be adopted temporarily (adjunctive drugs such as pirenoxine sodium eye drops may be used, but drugs cannot reverse opacity)
After surgery, standard use of antibiotic and anti-inflammatory eye drops (tobramycin/dexamethasone or pranoprofen).
safety_warnings: Do not wait until the cataract is 'fully mature' before surgery! Hypermature cataract can readily be complicated by phacolytic glaucoma or lens dislocation uveitis, increasing surgical difficulty and complication risk
Strictly prevent endophthalmitis after surgery (a catastrophic complication); within 1 week after surgery, avoid dirty water entering the eye and strictly prohibit eye rubbing and severe impact
In patients with diabetes, blood glucose must be strictly and stably controlled within a reasonable range before and after cataract surgery
personalization: Refractive cataract surgery: individualized selection of toric, bifocal, trifocal, or EDOF extended-range-of-vision intraocular lenses according to the patient's visual needs
Patients with concurrent high myopia: comprehensively screen for peripheral retinal degeneration and tears before surgery, and prevent retinal detachment during and after surgery
Patients with concurrent diabetic retinopathy: actively perform fundus laser photocoagulation before surgery and closely monitor for macular edema after surgery

skills.presentation: Acute attack of acute angle-closure glaucoma: sudden severe eye distension and eye pain in the affected eye, severe ipsilateral migraine, extremely rapid vision decline even to light perception only, accompanied by halos (iridescent rings around lights), nausea, and projectile vomiting; examination shows sharply elevated intraocular pressure (often >50mmHg, with the eyeball feeling hard as stone on palpation), mixed hyperemia, ground-glass corneal edema, extremely shallow anterior chamber, moderately dilated pupil in a vertical oval shape with absent light reflex; open-angle glaucoma has an insidious onset, is asymptomatic early, and in late stages shows progressive concentric visual field constriction ('tunnel vision').

first_questions: Did the severe eye pain or pressure and ipsilateral headache start suddenly? How many hours has the attack lasted?
Did your vision suddenly become markedly blurred? When looking at a glowing light bulb, do you see red and green rainbow-like halos around it (halos)?
Is it accompanied by severe nausea, vomiting, or even vomiting stomach contents? (often mistaken for acute gastroenteritis or a neurologic migraine)
followup_questions: Before the attack, had you stayed for a long time in a dark room (such as a movie theater or looking at a phone with the lights off), been excessively fatigued, or been extremely emotionally agitated?
Has the other eye previously had similar transient eye distension or foggy vision? Is there a family history of glaucoma?
Before symptom onset, did you use pupil-dilating eye drops (such as atropine) or take oral anticholinergic drugs?
stop_conditions: The features of acute angle-closure glaucoma—severe eye pain and headache, halos, nausea and vomiting, and acute vision decline—have been confirmed
Typical emergency signs of high intraocular pressure, such as eyeball hard as stone and dilated fixed pupil, have been identified
Dark-room triggers and the bilateral narrow-angle anatomical basis have been clearly assessed

essential: Intraocular pressure measurement (Goldmann applanation tonometer or non-contact tonometer, NCT; in the acute phase it often spikes to 50-80mmHg)
Slit-lamp microscopy examination (to assess the degree of corneal edema, peripheral anterior chamber depth by Van Herick grading, pupil shape, and light reflex)
Gonioscopy (to determine whether the anterior chamber angle is open or closed; the gold standard for differentiating open-angle from angle-closure glaucoma)
Visual acuity testing and funduscopic assessment of the optic nerve cup-to-disc ratio (C/D)
if_suspected: Visual field testing (automated Humphrey perimetry to detect characteristic glaucomatous visual field defects: arcuate scotoma, nasal step, and tunnel vision)
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) (accurate measurement of retinal nerve fiber layer, RNFL, thickness and optic disc parameters)
Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) (to assess fine anatomical structures of the anterior segment and the mechanism of angle closure)
avoid: During a suspected acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma, pupil-dilating drugs such as atropine and tropicamide are absolutely prohibited (they can cause complete angle closure and blindness)
Mistaking a patient with nausea and vomiting for having simple gastroenteritis and delaying emergency ophthalmologic intraocular pressure-lowering rescue

first_line: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency! Immediate race-against-time rescue to lower intraocular pressure is mandatory: hyperosmotic dehydrating agent (20% mannitol injection 250ml by rapid intravenous infusion, completed within half an hour)
Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (methazolamide tablets) or topical eye drops (brinzolamide eye drops)
Topical miotic (1%-2% pilocarpine eye drops applied frequently to constrict the pupil and open the angle)
Combined with topical beta-blockers (timolol eye drops) and alpha2-receptor agonists (brimonidine tartrate)
After intraocular pressure stabilizes and corneal edema resolves, first choice is laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) or trabeculectomy anti-glaucoma filtering surgery.
safety_warnings: Acute high intraocular pressure persisting for hours to days can cause irreversible ischemic necrosis of the optic nerve and permanent total blindness; intraocular pressure must be lowered emergently

Pilocarpine may be ineffective when intraocular pressure is extremely high (>50-60mmHg) because of ischemic paralysis of the iris sphincter; systemic dehydration to lower intraocular pressure is needed before instilling the drug
Rapid intravenous infusion of mannitol requires caution regarding the risk of severe cardiac insufficiency/heart failure and renal failure in older patients
personalization: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG): first choice is prostaglandin eye drops (latanoprost/travoprost, once nightly) or selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT)
Angle-closure glaucoma in the preclinical and prodromal stages (fellow eye): perform prophylactic laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) early
Patients with severe bronchial asthma or severe bradycardia: non-selective beta-blockers (timolol) are strictly prohibited among topical intraocular pressure-lowering drugs

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden severe foreign body sensation, burning pain, and copious watery discharge in one or both eyes. Typical manifestations include eyelid redness and swelling and marked conjunctival hyperemia and edema, possibly with enlarged and tender preauricular lymph nodes. Some patients have photophobia, tearing, and mild blurred vision. The course is self-limited but highly contagious, and outbreaks often occur in collective settings or families.

first_questions: Which eye did the symptoms start in, or did both eyes become affected at the same time?
Recently, have you had contact with anyone with similar red eye, or have you been to a swimming pool?
Is the discharge watery or purulent?
followup_questions: If there is preauricular lymph node swelling and pain, ask further about the severity and duration of the pain.
If vision decline is marked, ask whether there is blurred vision caused by corneal involvement.
If symptoms persist for more than two weeks without improvement, ask further about a history of immunosuppression.
stop_conditions: Acute onset in one or both eyes has been clarified, with typical watery discharge and preauricular lymph node enlargement.
The patient has no severe systemic infection symptoms and no history of ocular trauma.
The epidemiologic exposure history is clear, and the clinical manifestations are consistent with seasonal epidemic features.

essential: Slit-lamp microscopy examination (to assess conjunctival hyperemia and pseudomembrane formation)
Fluorescein staining (to screen for punctate corneal epithelial loss)
Palpation of preauricular lymph nodes (to confirm enlargement and tenderness)
if_suspected: Conjunctival scraping cytology (to identify eosinophils or viral inclusion bodies)
PCR testing (to confirm adenovirus serotype)
Tear bacterial culture (to exclude concurrent bacterial infection)
avoid: Routine use of broad-spectrum antibiotic eye drops as first-line treatment (unless there is evidence of concurrent infection)
Unnecessary oral systemic steroids (may worsen viral infection spread)
Over-reliance on funduscopy (unless concurrent uveitis is suspected)

first_line: There are currently no specific antiviral drugs; treatment is mainly symptomatic and supportive. Cold compresses are recommended to reduce edema and pain, and artificial tears dilute the virus and relieve dryness. Do not use steroid-containing eye drops on your own, to avoid inducing corneal ulceration or prolonging the course. If secondary bacterial infection occurs, a fluoroquinolone eye drop may be added for short-term use. Pay attention to isolation to avoid cross-infection; it usually resolves spontaneously in 1-2 weeks.
safety_warnings: Contraindications: glucocorticoids are contraindicated in patients with active corneal ulcer or immunodeficiency.
Drug interactions: avoid frequent alternating use with preservative-containing eye drops, which can lead to additive toxicity.
Prevention of serious adverse reactions: be alert for steroid-induced ocular hypertension and secondary fungal infection.
personalization: Pediatric patients need strengthened caregiver guidance to prevent eye rubbing that can cause corneal damage.
Older adults or immunocompromised patients need close monitoring of disease progression to prevent complications.
Professional drivers or precision workers should be told to temporarily avoid driving or operating precision instruments.

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent burning, itching, and foreign body sensation at the eyelid margins of both eyes or one eye; on waking, scales or crusts may be seen at the base of the eyelashes, making it difficult to open the eyes. Some patients have photophobia, lacrimation, and blurred vision (due to tear film instability). On examination, eyelid margin hyperemia and telangiectasia may be seen, eyelashes may fall out easily or become misdirected, and severe cases may develop ulcers or trichiasis. Symptoms often recur and are refractory to prolonged treatment.

first_questions: Do you have persistent burning, itching, or a foreign body sensation in your eyes?
When you wake up in the morning, are your eyelids stuck together, or is there a large amount of crusted discharge?
followup_questions: Do the symptoms worsen after prolonged near work or exposure to dust?
Do you have a recent history of facial acne, seborrheic dermatitis, or rosacea?
stop_conditions: Symptoms have been confirmed as chronic and recurrent, with no signs of acute purulent infection
An associated systemic skin disease history (such as seborrheic dermatitis) has been confirmed
The patient's vision is not severely affected and there are no signs of corneal involvement

essential: Smear microscopy of eyelashes and secretions
if_suspected: Demodex mite detection (pressure smear of secretions from the base of the eyelashes)
Schirmer test for tear secretion
Meibomian gland function assessment (expression to observe lipid characteristics)
avoid: Routine fundus examination (unless concurrent keratitis affecting vision is suspected)
Unnecessary systemic antibiotic blood cultures
Non-indicated orbital CT or MRI scans

first_line: First-line treatment is mainly local hygiene care: hot compresses 2-4 times daily (40-45°C, 10-15 minutes) combined with eyelid margin cleaning (wiping the base of the eyelashes with dedicated wipes or diluted baby shampoo). Pharmacotherapy includes erythromycin ophthalmic ointment or tobramycin dexamethasone eye drops (short-term use); if Demodex mite infection is also present, metronidazole gel should be added. The course usually lasts 2-4 weeks; after symptom relief, low-frequency maintenance care should be maintained to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of steroid-containing eye drops to prevent glaucoma or cataract
Erythromycin preparations are contraindicated in patients allergic to macrolide antibiotics
If severe pain or sudden vision loss occurs during medication, stop the drug immediately and seek medical attention
personalization: Use steroid drugs with caution in pediatric patients; prefer antibiotic eye ointment
Pregnant and breastfeeding women need medication types adjusted under medical guidance
Elderly patients with dry eye need combined artificial tears to improve tear film quality

skills.presentation: Patients often report a painless, slowly enlarging hard nodule on the eyelid, with normal or slightly red overlying skin. Some patients develop astigmatism due to compression of the eyeball by a large mass, causing blurred vision, or when secondary infection occurs, redness, swelling, heat, pain, and purulent discharge appear. The course is usually weeks to months, with no obvious systemic symptoms.

first_questions: How long has the eyelid mass been present? How fast is it growing?
Do you have local pain, tenderness, or redness, swelling, or warmth?
Have you had decreased vision or blurred vision recently?
followup_questions: If there is pain, have you squeezed it or applied hot compresses yourself?
Have you had recurrent hordeolum or a history of blepharitis?
Does the mass affect eye opening or rub against the cornea and cause foreign body sensation?
stop_conditions: The nature of the mass has been confirmed as a painless hard nodule with no signs of acute inflammation
It has been confirmed that there is no visual impairment and no risk of serious complications
The patient has clearly described the disease course and previous related ocular history

essential: Eyelid palpation (assess hardness, mobility, and fluctuation)
Evert the eyelid to examine the conjunctival surface for granulation tissue
if_suspected: Ocular B-scan ultrasonography (for differentiation of deep or large cysts)
Pathologic biopsy (for elderly patients or recurrent refractory cases to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma)
avoid: Routine complete blood count (not needed in non-acute infection phase)
Unnecessary CT or MRI scans (unless deep orbital invasion is suspected)

first_line: Small early lesions are preferably treated conservatively: hot compresses 4 times daily (10-15 minutes each) to promote absorption, combined with artificial tears to relieve discomfort. If infection is present, short-term antibiotic eye ointment (such as erythromycin ophthalmic ointment) may be used. For larger masses that persist for more than 1 month without resolution, chalazion curettage is required, and the cyst wall should be completely removed during surgery to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: Do not forcibly squeeze the lesion before it matures, to avoid spread of infection causing orbital cellulitis
Patients with diabetes should be alert to poor postoperative wound healing and infection risk
Avoid long-term use of steroid-containing eye drops, which can increase intraocular pressure
personalization: Pediatric patients often require surgery under general anesthesia to reduce fear and difficulty with cooperation
In elderly patients, if the mass is hard and fixed, it must be sent for pathology to exclude malignancy
For recurrent patients, it is recommended to also treat blepharitis and regulate meibomian gland function

skills.presentation: Patients often report long-standing tearing, which worsens outdoors or in wind. Eczematous changes or redness and swelling may be seen on the skin at the medial canthus, and pressure over the lacrimal sac area may cause mucoid or purulent discharge to reflux from the punctum. Some patients have mild distending pain at the medial canthus. The course is prolonged with recurrent episodes, and antibiotic eye drops only temporarily relieve symptoms.

first_questions: How long has your tearing lasted? Is it accompanied by increased ocular discharge?
When you press below the inner corner of the eye (medial canthus), does pus flow out or is there discomfort?
followup_questions: Have you had a recent acute episode, such as local redness, swelling, heat, and pain?
Have you ever undergone nasolacrimal duct probing or eye surgery?
stop_conditions: The duration of tearing, the character of the discharge, and the response to lacrimal sac pressure have been clearly elicited
A history of prior treatment and any acute episodes has been obtained
The patient's presentation is typical and there is no systemic disease interfering with diagnosis

essential: Palpation and pressure test over the lacrimal sac area
if_suspected: Dacryocystography
Nasal endoscopy
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to exclude acute infection)
avoid: Routine fundus examination (not essential for diagnosis)
Unnecessary systemic CT scanning (unless tumor is suspected)
Blind nasolacrimal duct probing without imaging assessment

first_line: In the acute phase, first-line treatment is topical antibiotic eye drops combined with oral antibiotics to control infection

In the chronic phase, surgical treatment is mainly adopted, including endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy or external dacryocystorhinostomy. The lacrimal sac should be cleaned before surgery, and the lacrimal duct should be irrigated regularly after surgery to prevent adhesions. Non-pharmacologic interventions include maintaining ocular hygiene and avoiding eye rubbing.
safety_warnings: Do not perform forcible lacrimal duct probing during acute inflammation, to avoid spread of infection.
Before using antibiotics, confirm no allergy history and be alert to emergence of resistant bacteria.
After surgery, closely observe for complications such as epistaxis or cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea.
personalization: Elderly patients need cardiopulmonary function assessment to tolerate general or local anesthesia surgery.
Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to promote wound healing.
Pregnant women should use systemic antibiotics with caution; prefer local treatment or postpone surgery.

skills.presentation: Patients usually report inability to distinguish specific colors, such as red-green confusion (difficulty distinguishing traffic lights or red and green objects), or in total color blindness, objects appear in grayscale and there is photophobia. Symptoms are mostly present from childhood, bilateral and symmetric, without pain or decreased vision, and abnormalities are seen only on color discrimination tasks.

first_questions: When did you first notice that you cannot distinguish certain colors?
Do you have difficulty seeing red and green lights, or other colors?
followup_questions: Does this color confusion affect your work or driving safety?
Does anyone else in your family have a similar condition?
stop_conditions: It is confirmed that symptoms have been present since childhood and are bilateral and symmetric
The main types of colors confused have been identified
Acquired causes have been excluded

if_suspected: Farnsworth-Munsell 100 hue test
Fundus photography and OCT examination
avoid: Visual field examination
Intraocular pressure measurement

first_line: Currently there is no cure. Genetic counseling is recommended, and occupations with high color vision requirements (such as pilot or electrician) should be avoided. Special filter glasses may help some patients distinguish colors, but the effect varies by individual. The focus is on psychological adaptation and environmental modification.
safety_warnings: Do not use unproven 'miracle drugs' or surgical therapies
Avoid relying on a single visual cue, which may lead to safety hazards
Note that temporary color vision changes caused by drugs need to be differentiated
personalization: Pediatric patients need early intervention and education to avoid academic frustration
Drivers need to be assessed for compliance with local regulatory standards
Provide alternative career planning guidance for those with limited occupational choices

skills.presentation: Patients often report painless, progressive vision loss, blurred vision, or double vision. Because an underlying disease (such as uveitis or glaucoma) is present, there may be accompanying eye redness, photophobia, or floaters. The degree of visual impairment is related to the activity of the underlying disease and the progression of lens opacity; in the early stage, it may manifest only as reduced contrast sensitivity, and in the late stage it can cause blindness.

first_questions: How long has your recent vision loss lasted? Did it occur suddenly or did it gradually worsen?
Do your eyes feel red, painful, or sensitive to light?
Have you previously been diagnosed with uveitis, glaucoma, or any other eye disease?
followup_questions: If you have eye pain, what is the nature and duration of the pain?
Is the vision loss associated with flare-ups of eye inflammation?
Are you currently using any eye drops or oral medications?
stop_conditions: The type of underlying disease and the extent to which cataract affects vision have been clarified.
The patient has clearly described the symptom progression and past treatment history.
It has been initially determined that emergency surgery is not required and further examinations can be arranged.

if_suspected: Intraocular pressure measurement (to rule out secondary glaucoma)
UBM or anterior segment OCT (to assess anterior chamber depth and ciliary body status)
Biometry (to calculate intraocular lens power)
avoid: Prolonged waiting and observation after pupillary dilation (strong mydriatics should be used with caution during inflammation)
Unnecessary systemic imaging (unless a systemic disease is suspected)
Direct laser treatment (before diagnosis is established)

first_line: Surgery is the first-line treatment, namely phacoemulsification combined with intraocular lens implantation. Before surgery, the underlying disease (such as uveitis) must be controlled and inactive for at least 3 months to reduce the risk of postoperative inflammatory response. During surgery, an appropriate intraocular lens is selected according to corneal endothelial status and anterior capsule condition. Postoperatively, glucocorticoid eye drops are routinely used for anti-inflammatory treatment, combined with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs when necessary; the course usually lasts 4-6 weeks until inflammation completely resolves.
safety_warnings: Surgery must not be forced during active uveitis, as it can easily lead to macular edema or retinal detachment.
Be alert to glucocorticoid-induced elevation of intraocular pressure, and intraocular pressure changes need to be monitored.
Be vigilant for postoperative infectious endophthalmitis, especially in immunosuppressed patients.
personalization: For pediatric patients, amblyopia training and the possibility of second-stage surgery should be considered.
For highly myopic patients, the risk of retinal detachment should be assessed, and fundus examination should be completed before surgery.
For patients with comorbid diabetes, blood glucose should be strictly controlled to prevent postoperative infection and macular edema.

skills.presentation: Affected children often present with photophobia, tearing, and blepharospasm, and parents often report that the child frequently rubs the eyes or closes the eyes. Typical signs are corneal opacity (hazy), enlarged eyeball (buphthalmos), and abnormally increased corneal diameter. In those with onset in infancy, because they cannot express decreased vision, the condition is easily mistaken for ordinary conjunctivitis; particular attention should be paid to whether persistent tearing and light sensitivity are present.

first_questions: Does your child frequently have tearing or light sensitivity?
Have you recently noticed that your child's eye is larger than usual or that the cornea looks white?
Is there any family history of glaucoma?
followup_questions: Is the tearing unilateral or bilateral? Is it accompanied by increased discharge?
Does the child frequently rub the eyes or appear irritable and crying?
Was there a history of difficult delivery or eye trauma at birth?
stop_conditions: Core symptoms such as photophobia, tearing, and corneal opacity have been clearly described
Family history has been confirmed and the timeline of onset is clear
The patient's age matches the typical onset stage and there is no interference from other systemic diseases

essential: Intraocular pressure measurement (non-contact tonometry or tonometry under anesthesia)
Slit-lamp examination (to assess corneal clarity and degree of edema)
if_suspected: Fundus examination (to assess optic nerve cup-to-disc ratio)
Ocular B-scan ultrasonography (to assess axial length and posterior segment structures)
Gonioscopy (gold standard, requires examination under anesthesia)
avoid: Cycloplegic refraction (may worsen the condition in the acute phase; decision should be made after physician assessment)
Routine fundus fluorescein angiography (not first-line; considered only in complex cases)
Systemic CT scanning (unless intracranial disease causing secondary glaucoma is suspected)

first_line: Surgery is the first-line treatment, such as trabeculotomy or trabeculectomy. Medications are only an adjunct for temporary preoperative intraocular pressure control; beta-blocker eye drops are commonly used. After surgery, intraocular pressure and corneal clarity need to be closely monitored to prevent complications. Nonpharmacologic interventions include regular follow-up and refractive correction to prevent amblyopia.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of high-concentration miotics to prevent induction of iridocyclitis
Pay attention to any history of drug allergy, especially to sulfonamide drugs
Be vigilant for the risk of choroidal detachment caused by postoperative hypotony
personalization: For premature infants, the anesthesia regimen and drug doses need to be adjusted
For children with syndromic disease, multidisciplinary collaboration is needed to formulate a comprehensive treatment plan
For patients with bilateral involvement, surgery should be performed in stages to avoid the risks of simultaneous anesthesia

skills.presentation: Patients often report that the eyelid cannot be lifted, obstructing the line of sight or requiring them to tilt the head back to see. Typical manifestations are a unilateral or bilateral upper eyelid margin lower than its normal position, covering part of the pupil, with deepened forehead wrinkles to compensate for levator muscle function. Affected children may have epicanthus, trichiasis, or signs of amblyopia. Symptoms are usually noticed shortly after birth, are non-fluctuating, and are unrelated to fatigue.

first_questions: Has the child had difficulty lifting the eyelid since birth?
When looking at things, does the child often need to tilt the head back or raise the eyebrows?
followup_questions: Is there a family history of similar eye disease?
Does the child have blurred vision, photophobia, or frequent eye rubbing?
stop_conditions: The time of onset (congenital) and main signs (degree of pupil coverage) have been clarified.
Acquired factors such as myasthenia gravis have been excluded (no diurnal variation with morning mildness and evening worsening).
Whether there is concomitant strabismus or risk of amblyopia has been confirmed.

essential: Visual acuity testing and refractive status assessment
Corneal reflex and ocular motility examination
if_suspected: Neostigmine test (to rule out myasthenia gravis)
Orbital CT or MRI (to screen for neurogenic lesions)
Synoptophore examination (to assess binocular visual function)
avoid: Routine complete blood count (non-infectious disease)
Unnecessary excessive screening before general anesthesia
Complex electrophysiologic testing in infants and young children

first_line: For mild cases that do not affect the visual axis, observation until 3-4 years of age is acceptable

For moderate to severe cases affecting visual development, surgery should be performed as early as possible. The first-line procedures are levator resection or frontalis suspension. Postoperatively, occlusion therapy should be used to treat amblyopia, and refractive status should be rechecked regularly. Nonpharmacologic interventions include instructing parents to avoid forcing the child to open the eyes, to prevent corneal exposure injury.
safety_warnings: Myasthenia gravis must be ruled out before surgery; otherwise, surgery is ineffective and may worsen the condition.
After surgery, corneal exposure should be closely monitored to prevent exposure keratitis.
Anesthesia risk: general anesthesia in infants and young children requires strict assessment of the airway and cardiopulmonary function.
personalization: Children with amblyopia should undergo amblyopia training first before or concurrently with surgery.
For severe levator function deficit, frontalis suspension is preferred over levator resection.
For bilateral asymmetry, the surgical plan should be individualized according to the dominant eye and cosmetic needs.

skills.presentation: Affected children present at birth or shortly after birth with whitening, grayish-white, or cloudy opacity of the black part of the eye (cornea), often accompanied by photophobia, tearing, and blepharospasm. In some cases, enlargement of the eyeball (buphthalmos) may be seen, suggesting concomitant congenital glaucoma. Parents often report that the child's eye is opaque, that the child cannot see objects clearly, or that the child is extremely sensitive to bright light, with severely impaired visual development.

first_questions: Did the child's eye look white or cloudy at birth?
Does the child show obvious light sensitivity, tearing, or frequent eye rubbing?
Is there a family history of similar eye disease or genetic disease?
followup_questions: If abnormal eye enlargement is found, ask further: 'Have you recently noticed that the child's eye is getting larger or that the child is crying more?'
If systemic symptoms are present, ask further: 'Does the child have hearing loss, heart problems, or other developmental delay?'
If the disease is unilateral, ask further: 'Is the vision or appearance of the other eye normal?'
stop_conditions: The extent of opacity, whether it involves all layers, and whether glaucoma is concomitant have been clarified
The presence or absence of symptoms related to a systemic syndrome has been confirmed
Information on the need for key imaging examinations has been obtained

if_suspected: UBM (ultrasound biomicroscopy)
Anterior segment OCT
Genetic testing (for suspected syndromic forms)
avoid: Routine cycloplegic refraction (may worsen discomfort in the acute phase and is not first-line)
Unnecessary systemic CT/MRI (unless intracranial disease is highly suspected)

first_line: Treatment depends on the cause and the degree of opacity. For isolated opacity, penetrating or lamellar keratoplasty can be performed

If congenital glaucoma is concomitant, trabeculotomy or goniotomy should be performed first to control intraocular pressure, and keratoplasty should be performed after the condition is stabilized. Long-term follow-up is required after surgery to prevent rejection and secondary glaucoma, along with amblyopia training.
safety_warnings: Keratoplasty must not be performed when intraocular pressure is uncontrolled
When immunosuppressants are used, infection risk and bone marrow suppression require close monitoring
Postoperatively, be vigilant for graft edema and failure caused by elevated intraocular pressure
personalization: Infants and young children require general anesthesia for detailed examinations and surgery
For bilateral disease, the eye with poorer vision should be treated first, and amblyopia intervention should be started as early as possible
For patients with concomitant systemic syndromes, multidisciplinary collaboration is needed to formulate a comprehensive treatment plan

skills.presentation: Children often present with inward turning of the eyelids in one or both eyes, with eyelashes rubbing against the cornea. Typical complaints include frequent blinking, photophobia, tearing, and eye rubbing. Infants and young children may cry and become irritable due to ocular discomfort. Examination may show the lower eyelid margin rolling toward the eyeball; some patients have conjunctival hyperemia and punctate corneal epithelial loss, and severe cases may develop corneal ulceration.

first_questions: Does the child frequently rub the eyes or tear?
Does the child show photophobia or difficulty opening the eyes?
Did the symptoms begin at birth or appear recently?
followup_questions: If tearing is mentioned, ask whether there is purulent discharge?
['If photophobia is mentioned, ask whether it is accompanied by decreased vision or whitening of the black part of the eye?']
['If eye rubbing is mentioned, ask whether there is a history of trauma or family history of inherited disease?']
stop_conditions: Typical entropion signs (such as trichiasis) have been clearly described, and there is no evidence of complications.
The parents have provided a complete birth history and past ocular history.
The duration of symptoms and aggravating factors have been fully confirmed.

essential: Assessment of eyelid position and eyelash direction
if_suspected: Lacrimal irrigation (to rule out lacrimal duct obstruction)
Corneal topography (to assess the extent of corneal damage)
Intraocular pressure measurement (to rule out secondary glaucoma)
avoid: Routine fundoscopy (not necessary in the non-acute phase)
Whole-body CT scan (unless a syndrome is suspected)
Unnecessary prescription of antibiotic eye drops

first_line: For mild cases, conservative treatment is preferred, including use of artificial tears multiple times daily to lubricate the cornea and prevent corneal dryness.

Combine with massage therapy; instruct parents to push the lower eyelid skin downward to correct the position. If conservative treatment is ineffective or corneal damage is significant, surgical correction such as suture technique or skin excision should be considered after age 3-4 years.
safety_warnings: Do not use corticosteroid-containing eye drops on your own, as this may induce glaucoma.
Avoid excessive force during massage, which may cause eyelid skin injury.
Be alert to the risk of corneal ulcer perforation and ensure close follow-up.
personalization: Premature infants require more frequent monitoring of corneal status.
Patients with concomitant strabismus require simultaneous assessment of eye alignment.
Use irritating lubricants with caution in patients with an allergic constitution.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of sudden eye pain, severe foreign-body sensation, photophobia, tearing, and blurred vision. Typical findings include blepharospasm, marked conjunctival hyperemia, punctate or patchy corneal infiltrates and ulcers, and positive fluorescein staining. Some patients have increased discharge or floaters; symptoms usually begin unilaterally and progress rapidly.

first_questions: When did the eye pain and foreign-body sensation begin?
Have you had any recent eye trauma or worn contact lenses?
Is the decreased vision accompanied by marked photophobia and tearing?
followup_questions: If there is discharge, please describe its color and character (e.g., purulent, watery).
Have you recently had a cold, fever, or contact with patients with similar symptoms?
Do you have a history of dry eye, recurrent keratitis, or autoimmune disease?
stop_conditions: History of trauma, contact lens wear, and typical symptom manifestations have been clearly established.
The patient has described the complete course of illness and associated systemic symptoms.
Key information needed for initial differential diagnosis (such as source of infection and allergy history) has been collected.

essential: Visual acuity and intraocular pressure measurement
if_suspected: Corneal scraping smear and bacterial/fungal culture
Confocal microscopy
Anterior chamber paracentesis fluid analysis
avoid: Routine fundoscopy (unless posterior segment involvement by complications is suspected)
Unnecessary systemic imaging scans
Blind use of corticosteroid eye drops

first_line: Choose anti-infective drugs according to etiology: for bacterial infection, use levofloxacin eye drops every 1-2 hours.

For fungal infection, use natamycin eye drops 4-6 times daily. For viral infection, apply acyclovir ophthalmic ointment topically. At the same time, give artificial tears to relieve discomfort and, if necessary, oral analgesics. The course usually continues until 3-5 days after symptoms resolve; do not stop medication on your own.
safety_warnings: Do not use glucocorticoids before fungal infection has been ruled out, as this may worsen the condition.
Be aware of the risk of antibiotic resistance and avoid long-term misuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics without indication.
Be alert to drug-induced corneal disease and monitor for toxic reactions from long-term use of preservative-containing eye drops.
personalization: Pediatric patients should use preservative-free formulations, and dosing frequency should be adjusted.
Quinolones and aminoglycosides are contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women.
Immunosuppressed patients require a prolonged course and combined systemic anti-infective treatment.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of severe eye pain, photophobia, tearing, and decreased vision, accompanied by a marked foreign-body sensation. Examination may show grayish-white infiltrates on the corneal surface with blurred edges, and a central ulcer crater may form; some cases are accompanied by hypopyon or conjunctival hyperemia. Symptoms progress rapidly, and infectious causes such as bacterial, fungal, or amoebic infection should be considered.

first_questions: Have you had any eye trauma or worn contact lenses?
How long have the symptoms been present? Are they gradually worsening?
Have you had increased discharge or sudden decrease in vision?
followup_questions: If there was trauma, please describe when and how the injury occurred.
If you wear contact lenses, have you ever cleaned them improperly or worn them longer than recommended?
Do you have any systemic disease (such as diabetes) or an immunosuppressed state?
stop_conditions: The duration of symptoms and triggering factors have been clearly established.
The patient has described typical signs (such as corneal infiltrates and hypopyon).
An initial judgment has been made as to whether the cause is infectious or non-infectious.

if_suspected: Confocal microscopy (when fungal or amoebic infection is suspected)
Anterior chamber paracentesis fluid culture (for suspected severe infection)
Schirmer test (to rule out dry eye-related factors)
avoid: Routine fundus examination (unnecessary and may delay diagnosis)
Unnecessary systemic imaging examinations
Empirical antibiotic treatment without culture

first_line: Immediately start topical broad-spectrum antibiotic eye drops (such as levofloxacin) every 1-2 hours, and adjust medication according to culture results. If fungal infection is suspected, use natamycin or voriconazole eye drops. At the same time, give artificial tears to relieve discomfort and, if necessary, oral analgesics. The course is usually 2-4 weeks, until the ulcer heals.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term use of corticosteroid-containing eye drops to prevent worsening of infection.
Check for a history of drug allergy to prevent allergic reactions.
Closely monitor the risk of corneal perforation and intervene promptly.
personalization: Pediatric patients require adjusted drug doses and strengthened care guidance.
Patients with diabetes need strict glycemic control to promote healing.
Immunosuppressed patients should have a prolonged observation period and combined systemic anti-infective treatment.

skills.presentation: Patients complain of redness, swelling, pain, and tenderness of the upper outer eyelid, often with inferomedial displacement of the globe. In the acute phase, conjunctival hyperemia and edema may be seen, and some patients have systemic symptoms such as fever and headache; chronic or recurrent cases present with a painless mass or recurrent swelling. If lacrimal secretory function is involved, dry eye symptoms such as foreign-body sensation and burning may occur.

first_questions: When did the redness, swelling, and pain in your eye begin? Did they start suddenly or worsen gradually?
Besides eye discomfort, have you recently had fever, a cold, or other symptoms of infection?
Have you had similar eyelid swelling before?
followup_questions: If there is decreased vision or restricted eye movement, please describe the specific manifestations.
Have you recently had trauma, surgery, or a habit of wearing contact lenses?
Do you have a history of autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Sjögren's syndrome?
stop_conditions: The features of acute bacterial infection and chronic granulomatous lesions have been clearly distinguished.
Complete past medical history and associated systemic symptoms have been obtained.
The patient's complaints are typical and there is no need for complex differential diagnosis.

essential: Palpation of the lacrimal gland region and assessment of eyeball position
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein testing
if_suspected: Orbital CT or MRI (to evaluate for abscess or tumor)
Autoantibody panel screening (such as ANA, RF)
Tear secretion test (Schirmer test)
avoid: Blind incision and drainage (before tumor has been ruled out)
Non-specific topical antibiotic instillation (when there is no clear evidence of bacterial infection)
Excessive imaging examinations (repeated CT/MRI when there are no signs of a space-occupying lesion)

first_line: For acute bacterial dacryoadenitis, the first choice is a susceptible antibiotic: oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 500mg every 8 hours for 7-10 days.

Severe cases require intravenous administration. Apply warm compresses to promote resolution of inflammation. If viral or autoimmune, give antiviral drugs or pulse glucocorticoid therapy according to the etiology. At the same time, use artificial tears to relieve dry eye symptoms.
safety_warnings: β-lactam drugs are contraindicated in patients allergic to penicillins; macrolides should be used instead.
Long-term glucocorticoid use requires intraocular pressure monitoring to prevent the risk of glaucoma and cataract.
Avoid squeezing the affected area yourself to prevent spread of infection into the orbit or cranium.
personalization: Pediatric patients require antibiotic dose adjustment according to body weight.
Use quinolones and tetracyclines with caution in pregnant women; penicillins are preferred.
In elderly patients, pay attention to hepatic and renal function and adjust doses of drugs metabolized by the liver or kidneys.

skills.presentation: Patients complain of inability to close the eyelids, often with tearing, photophobia, and ocular foreign body sensation. The typical manifestation is outward turning of the lower eyelid, with the conjunctiva exposed to air, leading to dryness and hyperemia. In severe cases, corneal ulceration may occur, accompanied by persistently increased discharge and blurred vision. Symptoms are often progressively worsening, and incomplete eyelid closure is particularly pronounced in the morning.

first_questions: Do your eyes feel dry, or do they constantly water?
Can you completely close your eyes? During sleep, has a family member noticed that your eyelids are not fully closed?
followup_questions: Did this symptom start suddenly or gradually worsen?
Have you had facial trauma, burns, or eye surgery?
stop_conditions: The degree of ectropion and associated corneal damage have been clearly determined
The cause has been confirmed (such as scarring, involutional, or paralytic)
The patient has clearly described the past treatment history and allergy history

if_suspected: Facial nerve function assessment (Bell phenomenon and observation of forehead wrinkles)
Eyelid skin elasticity test
Orbital CT (when tumor compression is suspected)
avoid: Routine fundus examination (when non-emergent and without retinal symptoms)
Unnecessary systemic blood immune screening
Blind tonometry (unless glaucoma risk is present)

first_line: For mild cases, artificial tears and lubricating eye ointment are first-line to protect the cornea; at night, moisture chamber spectacles or tape may be used to assist eyelid closure. Moderate to severe cases require surgery, including lateral tarsal strip suspension, medial canthal ligament tightening, or full-thickness skin grafting. After surgery, continued use of antibiotic eye ointment is needed to prevent infection, with regular review of corneal healing; the course is usually several weeks to months.
safety_warnings: Do not forcibly suture the eyelids when there is active corneal ulceration
Avoid long-term use of eye drops containing preservatives, which may cause toxic keratitis
Be alert to further vision loss caused by postoperative bleeding or infection
personalization: For older adults, assess systemic coagulation function to prevent intraoperative bleeding
For patients with facial palsy, combine with neurology treatment of the underlying disease
For pediatric patients, consider the impact of growth and development on the surgical approach

skills.presentation: Patients often complain that the visual axes of the two eyes are not parallel, with one eye deviating outward, especially noticeable when fatigued, inattentive, or when closing one eye in sunlight. Some patients report diplopia (double vision), reading difficulty, easy visual fatigue, or headache. Children may present with head tilt to compensate for diplopia, while adults often seek care because of abnormal appearance or vision problems.

first_questions: Have you noticed that one eye sometimes drifts outward, especially when you are tired or daydreaming?
Do you have double vision, headache, or easy fatigue when reading?
Did this symptom appear recently or has it been present since childhood?
followup_questions: In bright light, do you need to close one eye to see clearly?
Do you have a compensatory head tilt or facial asymmetry?
Is there a family history of similar eye disease?
stop_conditions: The timing pattern of the deviation and associated symptoms (such as diplopia and photophobia) have been clearly determined.
The onset time, frequency, and whether there is a history of trauma or neurological disease have been understood.
The patient has clearly described the degree of impact on daily life (such as reading and driving).

essential: Cover-uncover test and alternate cover test
if_suspected: Fundus examination (to rule out retinopathy)
Neuroimaging examination (CT/MRI, when a central cause is suspected)
Stereoacuity examination
avoid: Systemic blood tests without indication
Unnecessary invasive ocular biopsy
Direct surgical planning before refractive status has been assessed

first_line: Choose according to age and type: for children, spectacle correction of refractive error is first-line, combined with amblyopia training

Intermittent exotropia may be managed with vision training or prism glasses. If the deviation is stable and affects appearance or function, consider surgery (such as lateral rectus recession); regular follow-up after surgery is needed to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: Avoid overcorrection causing esotropia or worsened diplopia
Before surgery, assess general anesthesia risk and coagulation function
After surgery, prevent infection and control intraocular pressure fluctuations
personalization: For pediatric patients, prioritize ensuring the development of binocular visual function and avoid surgery too early
For older adults, assess the impact of comorbidities such as cataract on the surgical plan
For those with high refractive error, fully correct it first before assessing the strabismus angle

skills.presentation: Patients often present with monocular or binocular visual acuity significantly below the age-matched standard and not correctable with conventional spectacles. The chief complaint is often 'blurred vision' or 'cannot see details clearly,' but typical eye pain or redness is absent. Infants and young children may show sluggish response to visual stimuli, nystagmus, or strabismus. The key identifying point is that the decrease in visual acuity is disproportionate to the degree of refractive error, and there is a history of deprivation factors such as congenital cataract or ptosis.

first_questions: Has the child had any eye surgery or been found to have eye abnormalities from birth to now?
Do you usually notice the child squinting, tilting the head to see, or having involuntary eye shaking?
Is there a family history of amblyopia, strabismus, or high myopia?
followup_questions: If blurred vision is mentioned, ask: Is the blurring constant or does it come and go?
If ptosis is noted, ask: Does the eyelid often cover the pupil, especially worsening when tired?
Ask the parents whether occlusion therapy or glasses have been tried and what the effect was.
stop_conditions: A cause of form deprivation such as congenital cataract, severe ptosis, or corneal opacity has been clearly identified.
Visual acuity examination shows that best-corrected visual acuity is significantly below the normal value for age and cannot be explained by refractive error alone.
The child's cooperation is extremely poor, making detailed history-taking impossible, but the signs already highly suggest this disease.

essential: Best-corrected visual acuity examination (including visual acuity charts and fixation preference testing)
Slit-lamp microscopy examination (to assess the lens, corneal clarity, and eyelid position)
Fundus examination after pupillary dilation (to rule out retinal disease and assess macular development)
if_suspected: Ocular B-scan ultrasound (when refractive media opacity prevents a clear view of the fundus)
Visual evoked potential (VEP) examination (objective assessment of visual pathway function)
Axial length measurement (to help differentiate pathologic myopia or other organic disease)
avoid: Unnecessary systemic CT or MRI (unless intracranial tumor compressing the optic nerve is suspected)
Direct detailed refraction without pupillary dilation (susceptible to accommodation interference)
Blind use of atropine for pupillary dilation (caution in those at risk for acute glaucoma, although rare but noteworthy)

first_line: The primary treatment is to relieve form deprivation, such as cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation for congenital cataract, or ptosis correction. Amblyopia training should begin immediately after surgery, including patching the healthy eye (2-6 hours daily, adjusted by age and severity) and fine visual tasks (beading, tracing, etc.). The course usually lasts months to years, with regular follow-up of visual acuity and refractive status to prevent recurrence.
safety_warnings: After surgery, strictly prevent infection and secondary glaucoma, and monitor intraocular pressure changes.
During patching treatment, closely observe the visual acuity of the healthy eye to prevent reverse amblyopia.
Anesthesia risk: infants and young children undergoing general anesthesia require assessment of cardiopulmonary function and airway status.
personalization: For those with onset in infancy and early childhood, the treatment window is short, so early intervention is needed, and parental adherence should be emphasized.
For those with severe bilateral deprivation, patching is not appropriate; priority should be given to improving binocular visual input, supplemented by binocular dissociation training.
For those with concomitant strabismus, strabismus correction surgery should be performed at an appropriate time after amblyopia improves to restore binocular visual function.

skills.presentation: Patients often complain of markedly decreased night vision (nyctalopia), gradually developing visual field defects with tunnel vision. Some types are accompanied by blurred central vision, abnormal color vision, or metamorphopsia. Symptoms usually have an insidious onset and slowly worsen with age, and may be accompanied by photophobia or floaters. There is often a family history of similar eye disease.

first_questions: Do you have difficulty seeing things at night?
Is your vision loss in both eyes at the same time or in one eye? How fast is it progressing?
Does any other family member have similar vision problems or blindness?
followup_questions: Besides night blindness, do you feel that the peripheral range of your vision has narrowed?
Recently, have you had difficulty distinguishing colors or metamorphopsia?
Did the symptoms begin in childhood or only in adulthood?
stop_conditions: Typical features of night blindness, visual field constriction, and family history have been clearly asked about and recorded.
The patient has clearly described the onset time and progression of symptoms, and there is no history of acute ocular trauma.
The preliminary judgment is consistent with hereditary retinal disease, and further differentiation from acute inflammation or toxic factors is not needed.

if_suspected: Perimetry (to assess the degree of visual field defect)
Genetic testing (to determine the specific pathogenic gene mutation)
Fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA)
avoid: Routine head CT or MRI (unless an intracranial space-occupying lesion compressing the visual pathway is suspected)
Nonspecific systemic immune marker screening (when there is no evidence of infection or autoimmunity)
Unnecessary full coagulation panel before anticoagulant therapy (when there is no surgical indication)

first_line: There is currently no curative treatment; supportive therapy and slowing progression are the main approaches. Vitamin A palmitate supplementation is recommended (the dose must be strictly controlled under medical advice to avoid toxicity), and low-vision aids should be worn to improve quality of life. For specific gene mutations (such as RPE65), gene replacement therapy may be considered. Regular follow-up should monitor complications such as macular edema or cataract, with laser or surgical treatment when necessary.
safety_warnings: Do not self-administer high-dose vitamin A, to prevent hepatotoxicity and increased intracranial pressure.
When using antioxidants, be alert to interactions with other drugs, especially anticoagulants.
If there is a rapid decline in vision or severe eye pain, immediately evaluate for emergencies such as retinal detachment.
personalization: For pediatric patients, focus on visual rehabilitation training and psychological support.
Women of childbearing age should be counseled on genetic risk and make reproductive plans.
For those with comorbid systemic diseases (such as metabolic syndrome), multidisciplinary joint management is needed.

skills.presentation: Patients often report diplopia, difficulty reading, eye strain and headache, or blurred vision when tired, ill, or unable to concentrate. Some patients describe needing to blink frequently or close one eye to see clearly; symptoms worsen after prolonged visual use and improve with rest. Children may present with skipping lines while reading, copying errors, or difficulty concentrating, but without persistent diplopia.

first_questions: Do you have double vision or a feeling of eye strain when looking at things?
Does this discomfort worsen significantly after prolonged reading or work?
followup_questions: When the symptoms occur, are they accompanied by headache or nausea?
Do you need to rub your eyes frequently or close one eye to see clearly?
stop_conditions: The association between symptoms and visual fatigue has been clarified.
The duration of symptoms and relief methods have been understood.
Acute ocular trauma or neurologic emergencies have been ruled out.

if_suspected: Synoptophore examination
Accommodative function testing
Binocular vision assessment
avoid: Routine fundus fluorescein angiography
Head CT/MRI (in the absence of neurologic signs)

first_line: First-line treatment is non-surgical intervention, including vision therapy to enhance fusion.

If refractive error is present, full correction with glasses is required. For symptomatic esophoria or exophoria, prism correction may be attempted to reduce symptoms. Follow-up every 3 months is recommended, with the regimen adjusted according to symptom improvement.
safety_warnings: Avoid excessive use of prisms, which may lead to dependence
High-intensity vision therapy must not be performed blindly before accommodative function has been evaluated
Differentiate phoria from paralytic strabismus to prevent misdiagnosis and delayed treatment
personalization: In pediatric patients, vision therapy should be prioritized to promote development of binocular visual function
In older adults, presbyopia should be considered, and the near prism power should be adjusted appropriately
In patients with high myopia or hyperopia, refractive status must be strictly corrected before assessing the strabismus angle

skills.presentation: Patients often report photophobia and glare in one or both eyes, with blurred vision especially under bright light. Slit-lamp examination shows sectoral or circular defects in the peripheral iris, exposing the posterior lens equator, and abnormal pupil shape (such as pear-shaped or cat-eye-like), possibly accompanied by decreased visual acuity and diplopia.

first_questions: Do you feel that your eyes are unusually sensitive to light?
Has your vision been normal since childhood, or have you recently noticed a change in pupil shape?
followup_questions: Do any family members have similar eye problems?
Are there associated congenital anomalies or developmental delay?
stop_conditions: The abnormal pupil shape and complaint of photophobia have been clarified.
No history of trauma has been confirmed, and the presentation is congenital.
Family history and systemic associated symptoms have been documented.

if_suspected: Ocular B-scan ultrasonography (to rule out lens dislocation)
Genetic testing (screening for WNT1 and other loci)
Systemic physical examination (to assess cardiac, renal, and other systemic anomalies)
avoid: Prolonged observation after routine pupillary dilation (may worsen photophobia)
Unnecessary CT/MRI (unless intracranial pathology is suspected)
Corneal topography (of limited diagnostic value for iris defects)

first_line: First-line treatment is non-pharmacologic intervention; tinted contact lenses or custom light-blocking lenses are recommended to relieve photophobia and glare. If refractive error is present, corrective glasses are required. For severe cases affecting appearance or vision, artificial iris implantation or iris pigment epithelium transplantation may be considered. Regular follow-up is needed to monitor glaucoma risk.
safety_warnings: Avoid strong mydriatics such as atropine to prevent precipitation of acute glaucoma
Surgery must be strictly aseptic to prevent infection leading to endophthalmitis
Intraocular pressure changes must be closely monitored postoperatively
personalization: In pediatric patients, non-invasive optical correction should be preferred, and surgery should be evaluated after adulthood
Patients with coexisting glaucoma require concomitant intraocular pressure-lowering medication
In patients with bilateral defects, attention should also be paid to reconstruction of binocular visual function

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe unilateral eye pain, marked photophobia, tearing, and foreign-body sensation, with significantly decreased vision. Examination may show blepharospasm, mixed conjunctival injection, and grayish-white corneal infiltrates or ulcers with positive fluorescein staining. Some patients have hypopyon or miosis; symptoms progress rapidly, and without timely treatment can lead to corneal perforation or permanent visual impairment.

first_questions: When did the eye pain and photophobia begin? Did they start suddenly or worsen gradually?
Have you had any recent ocular trauma (such as a branch scratch or metallic foreign body), or do you wear contact lenses?
followup_questions: If there is increased discharge, is it purulent or watery?
Do you have a history of herpes simplex virus infection or autoimmune disease?
stop_conditions: The precipitating factor (such as trauma or contact lens wear) has been clarified, and symptoms are typical.
No systemic immunosuppression or high-risk factors for special infections have been confirmed.
The degree of visual decline and extent of the corneal lesion have been clearly assessed through the initial interview.

essential: Visual acuity and intraocular pressure measurement
if_suspected: Corneal scraping smear and bacterial/fungal culture
Confocal microscopy
PCR testing for viral nucleic acid
avoid: Routine ophthalmoscopy (cannot be performed in the acute phase because of corneal opacity)
Blind use of corticosteroid eye drops
Unnecessary systemic CT scanning

first_line: Select sensitive antibiotics or antivirals based on etiologic results. For bacterial keratitis, fluoroquinolone eye drops (e.g., levofloxacin) are first-line, every 1-2 hours.
For fungal keratitis, corticosteroids are contraindicated; natamycin or amphotericin B should be used.

For viral (HSV) keratitis, acyclovir ophthalmic ointment or oral valacyclovir is first-line. The course should continue until 3-5 days after clinical symptoms have completely resolved, with artificial tears to promote healing. Patients must not discontinue medication on their own.
safety_warnings: Glucocorticoids must not be used before fungal infection has been excluded, to avoid infection spread and even corneal perforation.
Pay attention to history of drug allergy, especially allergy to sulfonamides or quinolones.
Be alert for corneal epithelial toxicity and emergence of resistant bacteria with long-term use.
personalization: In pediatric patients, dosing frequency should be adjusted and supervision strengthened to prevent eye rubbing from worsening the injury.
Contact lens wearers should stop wearing lenses immediately, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection should be specifically investigated.
In immunocompromised patients, the treatment course should be prolonged and combined with systemic anti-infective therapy.

skills.presentation: Patients often report rapid progression of myopia or astigmatism over a short period, with poor visual correction despite wearing glasses. Typical manifestations are blurred vision and ghosting (monocular diplopia) in one or both eyes, marked nighttime glare, and inability to improve vision despite frequent changes in spectacle prescription. In some patients, eye-rubbing habits worsen symptoms; be alert for acute corneal edema or scar formation caused by corneal thinning.

first_questions: Has your spectacle prescription changed rapidly over the past year? Do you change glasses frequently?
Do you have double vision or see halos around lights at night?
Do you habitually rub your eyes forcefully and frequently?
followup_questions: If vision suddenly decreases with eye pain, do you feel a foggy veil before the eyes (suggesting corneal edema)?
Is there a family history of similar visual problems or eye disease?
Are there associated allergic symptoms such as allergic rhinitis or asthma?
stop_conditions: Recent rapid change in refractive error and poor corrected visual acuity have been clarified.
A long history of eye rubbing and an atopic predisposition have been confirmed.
The symptoms described by the patient are consistent with features of progressive keratoconus.

if_suspected: Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT)
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (to observe Fleischer ring or Vogt striae)
Fundus examination (to rule out other blinding eye diseases)
avoid: Routine refraction and spectacle prescription as the sole diagnostic basis
Laser corneal refractive surgery before corneal thickness has been evaluated
Relying solely on subjective visual acuity chart testing while ignoring changes in refractive status

first_line: In the early stage, vision correction is mainly with rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lenses, which can improve irregular astigmatism. If the disease progresses rapidly, corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is first-line to strengthen the cornea and halt progression of the cone. Soft contact lenses should be avoided because they cannot effectively reshape the cornea. For advanced cases with severe corneal scarring or intolerance to RGP lenses, corneal transplantation should be considered.
safety_warnings: Refractive surgery that cuts the cornea, such as LASIK, must not be performed in patients with keratoconus, as it may lead to corneal perforation
Transient corneal haze or pain may occur after cross-linking, requiring close follow-up
Long-term use of corticosteroid eye drops may inhibit corneal healing and should be carefully evaluated
personalization: In adolescent patients, cross-linking should be preferred to halt progression rather than spectacle correction alone
In patients with severe allergy, allergic conjunctivitis should be controlled concurrently to reduce triggers for eye rubbing
Corneal shape may fluctuate during pregnancy; monitoring frequency should be increased and lens parameters adjusted

skills.presentation: Patients often report a sharp decline in night vision (night blindness), accompanied by photophobia, lacrimation, and eye pain. Early in the course, the conjunctiva appears dry and lusterless, and Bitot's spots appear; as the condition progresses, the cornea rapidly becomes cloudy and softened, appearing grayish-white or yellow-green, and in severe cases perforation may occur, leading to iris prolapse. It is often accompanied by manifestations of systemic malnutrition, such as dry skin and follicular hyperkeratosis.

first_questions: Have you recently had difficulty seeing at night?
Do your eyes feel noticeably sensitive to light, watery, or painful?
Has your diet recently lacked vitamin A-rich foods (such as liver and dark-colored vegetables)?
followup_questions: If severe eye pain or sudden vision loss is mentioned, ask: 'Do your eyes feel as if there is a foreign body or as if they are about to rupture?'
If chronic diarrhea or malabsorption is mentioned, ask: 'Do you have a history of chronic gastrointestinal disease or recent marked weight loss?'
Ask about a history of rickets or a long-term vegetarian diet.
stop_conditions: A history of night blindness has been clearly established and typical signs of keratomalacia (such as Bitot's spots or corneal ulceration) are found.
Severe systemic symptoms of vitamin A deficiency and dietary history are confirmed.
The patient has already developed emergency complications such as corneal perforation and requires immediate emergency management.

if_suspected: Fundus examination (to assess retinal lesions)
Complete blood count and trace element analysis
Stool routine examination (to screen for parasitic infection)
avoid: Unnecessary measurement of the depth of corneal fluorescein staining (unless assessing perforation risk)
Unnecessary whole-body CT scans

first_line: Immediately supplement with high-dose vitamin A. In the acute phase, give oral vitamin A (adults 200,000 IU/day for 3 consecutive days) or intramuscular injection of a water-miscible vitamin A formulation. At the same time, use antibiotic eye ointment to prevent secondary infection and wear an eye shield to protect the cornea. After the condition stabilizes, switch to a maintenance dose and adjust the diet, increasing intake of vitamin A-rich foods.
safety_warnings: Strictly prohibit excessive long-term use of vitamin A to prevent toxicity
Use high-dose vitamin A with caution in patients with hepatic impairment
Avoid concomitant use with oral medications containing retinoic acid to prevent additive toxicity
personalization: For infants and young children, calculate the dose strictly by body weight to prevent overdose
For pregnant women, use medication under close monitoring to avoid teratogenic risk
For patients with steatorrhea, preferentially choose water-miscible vitamin A formulations

skills.presentation: Patients often report sudden vision loss, blurred vision, or diplopia, and some have eye pain or photophobia. Examination may show absence of lens reflex in the pupillary area, and slit-lamp examination may reveal abnormal lens position, such as complete dislocation into the anterior chamber or vitreous cavity.

first_questions: Have you experienced sudden vision loss or diplopia?
Do you have a history of eye trauma or a family history of genetic disease?
followup_questions: Do your symptoms worsen after specific movements?
Do you have other eye discomfort such as pain or photophobia?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical symptoms and has no other complex medical history
There is enough information to determine that further specialty examination is needed
The patient cannot provide useful information, but symptoms are obvious

if_suspected: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
Corneal endothelial cell count
avoid: Routine X-ray examination
Unnecessary CT scans

first_line: Select surgical extraction and intraocular lens implantation according to lens position. If the lens is in the anterior chamber, emergency surgery is required to prevent glaucoma
If it is in the vitreous cavity, elective management may be performed. Postoperatively, administer anti-inflammatory drugs and arrange regular follow-up.
safety_warnings: Avoid medications that may cause pupillary dilation
Be alert to the risk of postoperative infection and strictly follow aseptic technique
Watch for the occurrence of secondary glaucoma
personalization: For pediatric patients, consider long-term visual development needs
For elderly patients, assess general health status to determine surgical timing
For patients with high myopia, pay special attention to the risk of retinal detachment

skills.presentation: Patients are often asymptomatic or have only mild blurred vision or eye fatigue. As the disease progresses, peripheral visual field constriction may gradually occur, and central vision loss may occur in advanced stages. Some patients may feel mild headache or eye discomfort due to elevated intraocular pressure, but most early cases are asymptomatic and need to be detected through professional examination.

first_questions: Do you have blurred vision or a feeling of visual field constriction?
Does anyone in your family have glaucoma?
followup_questions: Do you often feel eye fatigue or headache?
Do you have a history of long-term use of corticosteroid medications?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical symptoms and has no other complex medical history
The patient can provide a complete family history and medication history
The patient states that there is no further information to add

if_suspected: Optical coherence tomography (OCT)
Gonioscopy
avoid: Unnecessary systemic imaging
Nonspecific blood tests

first_line: First-line treatment includes intraocular pressure-lowering medications (such as prostaglandin analog eye drops), once daily, continued to control intraocular pressure. If necessary, a beta-blocker or carbonic anhydrase inhibitor may be added. For patients with poor medication control, laser trabeculoplasty or surgery may be considered. Regular follow-up is also recommended to monitor intraocular pressure and visual field changes.
safety_warnings: Avoid mydriatic drugs during an acute angle-closure glaucoma attack
Pay attention to drug interactions, especially when used with antihypertensive drugs
Be alert to severe adverse reactions such as bradycardia and bronchospasm
personalization: For elderly patients, adjust the dose to avoid the risk of hypotension
Use certain intraocular pressure-lowering drugs cautiously in pregnant and lactating women
For pediatric patients, individualize dosing according to body weight and age

skills.presentation: Patients often report progressive vision loss, visual field defects, or decreased color discrimination. Typical symptoms include painless visual loss, central scotoma, color vision abnormalities (such as red-green color blindness), and sluggish pupillary light reflex.
